cues.text: Counselor to Two Kings

Little can be said with certainty about Swithin's early life; his own biographers wrote generations after his death, and he appears in contemporary documents only as a signature on a handful of royal charters.

What the charters and later tradition agree on is that he served King Egbert of Wessex as a trusted counselor in ecclesiastical affairs, and was likely entrusted with the education of Egbert's son Ethelwulf.
When Ethelwulf succeeded his father as king, he had Swithin elected bishop of Winchester.
Ceolnoth, Archbishop of Canterbury, consecrated him to the see on 30 October 852—a consecration securely dated by the very charters that otherwise say so little else about him.
A Bishop on Foot
As bishop, Swithin made his diocesan visitations on foot rather than on horseback, a small but telling detail.
Later chroniclers preserved it as evidence of deliberately humble governance.
Writing over two centuries later, William of Malmesbury called him 'a treasury of all virtues,' singling out his humility and charity to the poor.
Tradition holds that at his urging King Ethelwulf donated a tenth of his royal lands to the Church—the so-called Decimation of 854.
It credits Swithin, more speculatively, with early involvement in educating Ethelwulf's youngest son, the future King Alfred the Great, who was still thirteen when Swithin died.
A Basket of Broken Eggs
The one story that survived from Swithin's own lifetime, rather than being invented for his later devotion, is small and domestic.
Watching workmen build a church on Winchester's east side, he saw an old woman's basket of eggs crushed in the crowd.
He gathered up the broken shells himself and — the story says — restored the eggs whole.

Whatever its precise historicity, later ages found the story fitting: a bishop remembered less for grand ecclesiastical politics than for stopping to notice, and to mend, the small misfortune of an ordinary woman selling eggs in a market crowd.
Death, Burial, and an Unwanted Translation
Swithin died on 2 July 862 and, at his own explicit request, was buried outside in the common churchyard.
This was not with honor inside the cathedral, but where — his instructions specified — passersby might walk over his grave and rain fall on it from the eaves above.

There his body remained for over a century, until 971, when the reforming Bishop Ethelwold of Winchester, working alongside Sts. Dunstan and Æthelwold, had Swithin's relics moved into the new cathedral as its patron.
According to persistent legend, the move was accompanied by forty days of violent storms.
The faithful read these as the humble bishop's posthumous objection to the honor he had specifically tried to avoid.
This was likely the origin of enduring English weather-lore that rain on his feast day predicts forty more days of the same.
Legacy
Whatever the truth of the rain legend, it has outlived nearly everything else about Swithin in popular memory, eclipsing even the substance of his quiet, competent episcopate.
We recognize in Swithin a reminder that humility, genuinely practiced, tends to resist the very honors later admirers want to heap on it.
He was a bishop who asked to be trodden underfoot in death and was answered, a century later, with a shrine and cathedral dedication.
English children still repeat a saying about him without knowing quite who he was.
